sections.body:
A savanna is a wide, warm land covered in grass, with a few trees standing here and there. It lies between the forest and the desert, and most of the savannas in the world are in Africa.

The savanna has two seasons, not four. In the **wet season** the rain falls, and the grass grows tall and green. In the **dry season** there is no rain at all for months, and the grass turns yellow and dry. In the dry season, animals must walk a long way for every mouthful of water.

Grass here grows back very fast. After the first rains, the plain turns green within days, and thousands of animals move in to eat it. This is why the savanna is never empty ground. It is a table that is laid and cleared every year.

The trees are the special part. An acacia tree often stands alone, or with only a few friends, and its flat top spreads wide to make shade. Under that shade the grass grows taller and cooler, and animals rest there in the middle of the day.

Every animal on the savanna is built for the heat. Long legs carry it above the hot grass. Big ears let the heat out. A giraffe can drink from the treetops. Some animals travel for hours to find water, and others can go several days without a drink.

The savanna is also a big stage. The grass eaters are the stars of the day, and the hunters are the ones who watch. Everything on this plain depends on everything else, because the grass feeds the zebra and the zebra feeds the lion.

By the end of this article you will know who eats whom, the words scientists use for these animals, and what happens on a savanna in one single day.
examples: The savanna is covered in tall grass.
In the wet season the rain makes everything green.
The lion is a hunter on the savanna.
sections.heading: What is the savanna?

sections.body:
Zebras eat grass and never stop moving. Their stripes hide them in the tall grass, where you see stripes and not an animal. A zebra must keep walking because biting flies bother it more when it stands still.

Giraffes eat the leaves of tall acacia trees. A giraffe's neck is about two metres long, and its tongue is long enough to pick leaves between the thorns. Giraffes can see a lion from very far away.

African buffalo graze in herds of hundreds. They are dangerous when they are worried, because they have big curved horns and they do not run away. A buffalo that is attacked turns round and charges.

Wildebeest have heavy shoulders and a sloping back. They graze in big herds and then run together. When the herd runs, the ground shakes.

Elephants eat grass, leaves and bark. They dig in dry riverbeds with their trunks until they find water, and other animals follow them. An old elephant remembers the way to water that a young one has never seen.

Gazelles and antelopes are small, quick and watchful. A gazelle can jump higher than its own height, and it lifts its head often to look for danger.

All of these animals are called **herbivores**, because they eat plants. They are the ones who make the savanna worth looking at.
examples: The zebra is eating grass, just like the wildebeest.
The giraffe is eating leaves high in the tree.
The gazelle lifts its head to look for the lion.
sections.heading: The great grass eaters

sections.body:
Lions are the best known hunters here. They hunt at night, because the dark hides them. A lion sleeps for most of the day, and its roar can be heard nearly eight kilometres away.

Cheetahs are the fastest animals on land. They can run at about 100 kilometres an hour, but only for a few seconds, so they have to choose the moment carefully. Cheetahs hunt in the daytime, because a cheetah that is caught by a lion at night has no chance.

Hyenas laugh, and the sound is nothing like a laugh. They live in families called clans, and they hunt as well as they clean up. A hyena can carry a big piece of meat faster than a lion can.

Jackals are smaller and cleverer. They hunt at night, and the female carries food back to her pups.

Not every hunter is a predator. **Vultures** circle high in the sky, looking for a meal that is already finished. They clean up the savanna, and without them the plain would be covered in old bones.

Oxpeckers sit on the back of a buffalo and eat the ticks that bite it. The buffalo gets a clean scratch, and the bird gets a meal. This is called a partnership, and both sides win.

Dung beetles roll balls of dung across the ground and bury them. The dung is full of seeds, and the beetle plants a tree by accident.
examples: The lion is sleeping in the shade until the sun goes down.
The cheetah runs very fast, but only for a short time.
The oxpecker rides the buffalo and eats the ticks.
sections.heading: The hunters of the savanna

sections.body:
People who study these animals use special words. Here are four of the most useful ones.

Savanna means an open grassland with trees scattered across it. It is not a forest and it is not a desert. It is the land in between.

A **herbivore** is an animal that eats plants. Zebras, giraffes, elephants and wildebeest are all herbivores. The word comes from the same root as herbs, which are green plants.

A **carnivore** is an animal that eats meat. Lions, cheetahs, hyenas and wild dogs are carnivores.

Migration means a long journey that animals make again and every year, usually to follow the rain and the new grass. The great wildebeest migration on the savanna is the largest animal journey on land. Thousands of animals walk thousands of kilometres, and they do it year after year, and they do not need a map.

There are more words worth learning. **Predator** means an animal that hunts other animals. **Prey** means the animal that is hunted. A **herd** is a group of animals that stay together, and a **pride** is a family of lions.
examples: The savanna is grassland, not forest.
The giraffe is a herbivore, and the lion is a carnivore.
The herd is migrating because the rain has moved.
sections.heading: The words scientists use

terms.example: The savanna is a wide field of grass with a few acacia trees.
terms.gloss: An open grassland with trees scattered here and there, between a forest and a desert.

terms.example: The elephant is a herbivore, so it eats grass and leaves.
terms.gloss: An animal that eats plants, such as a zebra, a giraffe or an elephant.

terms.example: The cheetah is a carnivore, so it hunts other animals.
terms.gloss: An animal that eats meat, such as a lion, a cheetah or a hyena.

terms.example: The wildebeest migration crosses the whole savanna.
terms.gloss: A long journey that animals make every year to follow the rain and the new grass.

sections.body:
The sun makes the rules here. When the sun moves, the animals move with it, and the whole day has a shape.

First comes **sunrise**. The night animals go to sleep, and the grazers start to eat. The zebras drink first, because they are the thirstiest, and they stand in the water while they watch for crocodiles.

Then comes **late morning**, and the heat begins to climb. The small animals rest in the shade of the acacia trees, and the bigger ones stand still in the shade of their own bodies.

At **midday** the sun is highest and hottest. Most animals sleep now, and they hardly move. A hunting day is not a day of running about.

In the **late afternoon** the animals get up. The hunters begin to look for the weak ones and the young ones, because those are the easiest to catch.

And at **night** the hunters work properly. The lions and the hyenas move quietly through the dark grass, and the elephant sets off on a long walk to find water it may not reach until morning.
examples: At sunrise the zebras go to the water hole.
At midday the animals sleep in the shade.
At night the lion hunts in the dark grass.
sections.heading: How a day passes on the savanna
steps: At sunrise the grazers wake up and drink.
In late morning the small animals rest in the shade.
At midday the sun is highest and most animals sleep.
In late afternoon the animals get up and move about.
At night the hunters hunt and the elephants walk to water.

sections.body:
Look closely at the ground on a savanna and it is busy. The huge animals get all the attention, but the small ones keep the whole system working.

Termites build mounds that can be taller than a child. The mounds are air-conditioned: the colony moves the hot air up and the cool air down, so the inside stays the right temperature. Birds and lizards sit near the mounds to eat termites.

Dung beetles roll dung into balls and bury them underground. Each beetle makes a nest and lays one egg in the ball. When the larva hatches, it has a ready meal, and the beetle has also planted a seed.

Honeyguide birds have an amazing partnership with people. A honeyguide points at a bee tree by fluttering, and the people open the hive and take some honey. The bird eats the wax and the leftover larvae, so both sides get a share.

Ants carry food to the colony in long lines, and they follow the same path over and over, because the path is marked with a scent that only ants can smell.
examples: Look at that termite mound, it is taller than me.
The dung beetle is rolling its ball home.
The honeyguide is showing us where the honey is.
sections.heading: The small animals doing the big jobs

item.summary: The savanna is a great open grassland full of grass eaters and hungry hunters. After reading this you can name the animals that live there, use the words scientists use for them, and explain what happens on a savanna in the space of one day.
item.title: Amazing Animals of the African Savanna
